papers.title: Near-infrared II emissive metal clusters: From atom physics to biomedicine
papers.abstract: Abstract Near-infrared II (NIR-II) imaging at 1100–1700 nm supports deep tissue penetration, low auto-fluorescence interruption, and high imaging resolution due to advances in attenuating photon scattering and absorption. For example, semiconductor quantum dots and carbon nanotubes as pioneer molecular probes were used for hind limbs and cerebrovascular imaging, and organic small molecules and polymers were employed for ultrafast and three-dimensional tumor vasculature imaging. Compared with the reported NIR-II fluorescence probe systems, the atomic-precision metal clusters with unambiguous geometry structure can make the most of the spatial coordination of metal atoms by artificial atom manipulation, thus improving the luminescent quantum yield with tunable emission wavelength. Meanwhile, the water soluble, renal cleanable, and highly stable features make them promising candidates for in vivo imaging. In this review, we aim to summarize the molecular and electronic structure, and optical properties of NIR-II emissive metal clusters. Meanwhile, we highlight their applications in brain, kidney, gastrointestinal imaging and tumor metastasis monitoring. We particularly reviewed recent advances on the biosafety of gold clusters at ultrahigh concentration. Present work will promote the development of NIR-II imaging and make a step towards the clinical application.

papers.title: Development of an ultra-high vacuum system for a cold atom physics rack in space
papers.abstract: Abstract We present the design and testing of the ultra-high vacuum (UHV) system, which is a key apparatus for the Cold Atom Physics Rack (CAPR) operated on the Chinese Space Station that allows study of ultracold atoms in microgravity. The simulation of the gas flow and experimental tests show that our UHV has a pressure of 3.4 × 10 − 9 Pa in the science chamber, two orders of magnitude lower than that of the 2D magneto-optical trap (2D-MOT) chamber. Moreover, we demonstrate that the system can not only self-sustain an equilibrium pressure for more than 1 month without power but also restore the desired pressure in the interaction zone. The loss dynamics of the trapped atoms are also measured to assess the performance of the UHV system.

papers.title: A Portable, Compact Cold Atom Physics Package for Atom Interferometry
papers.abstract: In this paper, we report the design, implementation and experimental results of a portable, compact cold Cs atom physics package for atom interferometer experiments. With the physics package, we trapped and deep-cooled Cs atoms to ultracold temperatures of $\lt$ $5 \mu \mathrm{K}$. The deep-cooling method used in this work is relatively simple and effective, with which we obtained controlled temperature adjustment between 5 and $80 \mu \mathrm{K}$. The portability of the physics package makes it suitable for implementing atom interferometry with various interrogation configurations and relative orientations. The system is also good for studies of compact cold atom frequency standards. With the Raman laser and light pulse manipulation system we developed in this work, this portable cold Cs atom physics package is being used for atom interferometer experiments in our laboratory.

summary: The literature covers fundamental and applied atom physics, including studies of diffusion at the atomic level and Rydberg atoms, as well as technological advances like ultra-high vacuum systems for cold atom experiments in microgravity and portable cold atom packages for interferometry. It also explores atomic-precision metal clusters for near-infrared biomedical imaging, leveraging atom manipulation to tune optical properties. These works highlight the breadth of atom physics, from precision measurement and quantum technology to interdisciplinary applications.
gap: The integration of atomically precise metal clusters, which exhibit tunable optical properties via artificial atom manipulation, into cold atom interferometry systems for enhanced quantum sensing remains unexplored, despite the potential to combine the precision of atomic-scale materials with quantum technology.
question: How can atomically precise metal clusters with tunable optical properties be integrated into cold atom interferometry systems to enhance quantum sensing capabilities?
hypothesis: Integrating atomically precise gold nanoclusters with tunable near-infrared absorption into the measurement beam path of a cold atom Mach–Zehnder interferometer will increase the phase sensitivity to accelerations, with the sensitivity enhancement factor scaling linearly with the optical density of the clusters at the atomic transition wavelength.
methodology: Employ the compact cold atom physics package for atom interferometry (Paper 5) to realize a Mach-Zehnder interferometer with Cs atoms. Synthesize atomically precise Au25 nanoclusters with tunable near-infrared absorption via ligand engineering (Paper 1) and insert a cuvette containing cluster solution into the Raman laser beam path. Measure the interferometric phase shift using a Ramsey fringe spectroscopy sequence while varying the cluster optical density by changing concentration. Evaluate the sensitivity enhancement by calculating the Allan deviation of the acceleration measurement, and compare the sensitivity improvement factor with the predicted linear dependence on optical density through linear regression analysis.
proposal: The field of atom physics spans fundamental studies and technological applications, including cold atom interferometry for precision sensing and atomically precise metal clusters with tunable optical properties. However, integrating these clusters into cold atom systems for enhanced quantum sensing remains unexplored. This research asks: How can atomically precise metal clusters with tunable optical properties be integrated into cold atom interferometry to enhance quantum sensing capabilities? We hypothesize that inserting atomically precise gold nanoclusters with tunable near-infrared absorption into the measurement beam path of a cold atom Mach–Zehnder interferometer will increase phase sensitivity to accelerations, with sensitivity enhancement scaling linearly with optical density. To test this, we will employ a compact cold atom physics package for Cs atom interferometry, synthesize Au25 nanoclusters with tunable absorption via ligand engineering, and introduce a cuvette containing cluster solution into the Raman beam path. We will measure interferometric phase shifts using Ramsey fringe spectroscopy while varying optical density, and evaluate sensitivity via Allan deviation, comparing enhancement with linear predictions. The expected contribution is a novel hybrid approach that combines atomically precise materials with quantum sensors, potentially achieving unprecedented acceleration sensitivity and advancing interdisciplinary atom physics.

evaluation.comments: The proposal is clearly articulated with a well-defined gap, hypothesis, and methodology. It logically integrates specific retrieved papers (Papers 1 and 5) to address an unexplored intersection. The approach is novel, combining atomically precise clusters with cold atom interferometry for enhanced sensing. Feasibility is high given existing setups but may encounter integration challenges. The proposal is strongly grounded in the literature.

baseline.proposal: We propose to develop a platform that integrates cold atom trapping and atom-by-atom manipulation to engineer NIR-II emissive metal clusters with atomic precision, enabling systematic investigation of structure-property relationships for advanced biomedical imaging.

evaluation.comments: The proposal clearly combines cold atom techniques with atomic-precision cluster assembly for NIR-II imaging, logically extending recent advances in both fields. While novel in integration, the individual components are established, making feasibility moderate. It aligns well with the provided papers on metal clusters, cold atom systems, and atom-by-atom observation, though Rydberg physics is less directly tied.
